author_claim: Paul thought out his text in Biblical Hebrew before translating it with great accuracy into Greek, rather than passively reproducing the Septuagint.
short_quote: Paulus zijn tekst eerst in het Bijbels-Hebreeuws heeft overdacht
qualification: Discovered during author's exegetical research on Romans since 1986.
notes: Baaij 2005:239. Sets out core thesis of Paul as an accurate retro-translator of Hebrew Scripture.

author_claim: Paul functioned as an expositor of Scripture par excellence whose exegetical instruments lead to a clear understanding of both Paul's preaching and the Scriptures themselves.
short_quote: de echte Paulus de schriftuitlegger is bij uitstek
qualification: Applies when interpreters adopt Paul's own Hebrew-grounded interpretive instruments.

author_claim: The grammatical analysis explicitly assumes that the Hebrew text known to Paul did not deviate from the Masoretic Text available today.
short_quote: de Hebreeuwse tekst die Paulus heeft gekend, niet heeft afgeweken van de Hebreeuwse tekst die ons ter beschikking staat, namelijk de Masoretische tekst
qualification: Explicit working premise; would be falsified if Paul's Vorlage diverged significantly.
notes: Baaij 2005:243. Foundational assumption of MT consistency.

author_claim: Paul's translation of tsedaqah by dikaiosyne expresses the restoration of the covenant relationship between God and the addressed human being.
short_quote: wil dus zoveel zeggen als "herstel van de relatie tussen God en de door Hem aangesproken mens"
qualification: Righteousness represents relational restoration initiated by God, not human merit.
notes: Baaij 2005:247. Defining tsedaqah in Rom 4:3 / Gen 15:6.

author_claim: Paul uses postpositive de in Romans 4:3 to grant extra grammatical emphasis to the preceding verb episteusen, highlighting active trust.
short_quote: om het voorafgaande [werk]woord extra nadruk te verlenen
qualification: Contrasts with standard translations that place Abraham first.
notes: Baaij 2005:248. Function of postpositive de in Rom 4:3.

author_claim: Paul intentionally replaces the Septuagint's pre-covenant name Abram with Abraham, designating the covenant partner who responds to God.
short_quote: Niet dus "Abram" (LXX), maar Abraham, de God antwoordende mens
qualification: Abraham is viewed as the covenant partner who responds to God's speech.
notes: Baaij 2005:248. LXX Abram vs Paul's Abraham.

author_claim: In contrast to Romans 9:33 and 10:11 where Paul constructs pisteuo with epi and dative, in Romans 4:3 he uses a simple dative without preposition.
short_quote: Paulus gebruikt immers niet pi,steuw evpi, cum dativo (zoals in Rom. 9:33; 10:11)
qualification: Demonstrates intentional variation in Pauline prepositional syntax across Romans.
notes: Baaij 2005:248. Syntactic comparison between Rom 4:3 and Rom 10:11 / 9:33.

author_claim: By constructing pisteuo with a simple dative lacking prepositions epi or eis, Paul places grammatical emphasis on God as the divine Cause and Initiator.
short_quote: Met pi,steuw cum dativo (zonder prepositie dus) legt Paulus de nadruk op de Veroorzaker
qualification: Applies to Rom 4:3 and 10:16; trust is initiated by God and accepted by humanity.
notes: Baaij 2005:248. Dativus causae interpretation of pisteuo to Theo.

author_claim: Relying uncritically on Septuagint translations obscures Hebrew syntax and leads commentators to teach the opposite of what Hebrew Scripture states.
short_quote: de mens het tegenovergestelde van wat de Schrift zegt
qualification: Polemical claim regarding uncritical reliance on LXX translations.
notes: Baaij 2005:253. Polemic against uncritical Septuagintal reading of Paul.
